title: Foundations of Data Science
text:
Data Science has become one of the fastest growing fields in recent years and mathematics, statistics, and computer science provide the foundations for a well-prepared and adaptable data scientist. Many students, especially first generation students, may not be aware of the opportunities and flexibility offered by a data science degree while those that choose a data science degree may not always see the connects between their foundational mathematics, statistics, and computer courses to their career goals and upper division course work.
This website serves as repository to help current mathematics, statistics, and computer science instructors to

Learn about the ways their topics connect to data science and learn more about data science, and

Access learning activities that can easily be integrated into their lower-division courses.

We will focus on the following courses which will assume the model defined by the C-ID to conform to California Community College, California State University, and University of California System requirements for the courses. Despite the focus on the Californian system of higher education, the courses and topics should be widely applicable beyond California.

Precalculus
Differential Calculus (I)
Integral Calculus (II)
Multivariable Calculus (III)
Introductory Linear Algebra
Introductory Statistics

In each topic, the ethical aspects of the data science topics will be included as an ethics module for the topic with applications to the classroom integration.These may include:

Dealing with data
Limits of models
Noise in data
Bias
Ethical issues with modeling
Social implications of data and models
Use of ChatGPT/LLMs and other AI tools

Each topic will include support for pedagogical practices for integrating the topics into the classroom using equity minded and inclusive practices. This can include activities such as:

Projects (problem-based learning)
Discussions (inquiry-based learning)
Group activities (active learning)

And may use any of the following tech tools

Colab/jupyter notebooks or Quarto.

Google docs, spreadsheets, etc.
Desmos, Geogebra, etc.

This project is funded by the CA Learning Lab: Data Science Grand Challenge

section: Connections to Data Science: Gradient Descent
text:
Connections to Data Science: Gradient Descent
Partial derivatives and the gradient (Course Content #4) connect directly to gradient descent through the gradient vector, which collects the rate of change of a multivariable function in each coordinate direction. Because the gradient points toward steepest ascent, its negative identifies the locally steepest direction of decrease; gradient descent follows this direction iteratively to approximate a local minimum. In data science and AI, this method is used to minimize loss functions defined over high-dimensional parameter spaces, providing the mathematical mechanism behind fitting regression models, training neural networks, and optimizing other learning systems.

title: Introduction Statistics
text:
1 Course Description
MATH 110 uses probability techniques, hypothesis testing, and predictive techniques to support decision-making. Students explore descriptive statistics, probability and sampling distributions, statistical inference, correlation and linear regression, analysis of variance, chi-square and t-tests, and technology-based statistical analysis. Applications use data from a broad range of disciplines.






NoteCourse Content






Summarizing data graphically and numerically
Descriptive statistics: measurement, measures of central tendency, and variation
Sample spaces and probability
Random variables and expected value
Sampling and sampling distributions
Discrete distributions, including the binomial distribution
Continuous distributions, including the normal distribution
The Central Limit Theorem
Estimation and confidence intervals
Hypothesis testing and inference, including one- and two-population t-tests and the chi-square test
Correlation, regression lines, and analysis of variance (ANOVA)
Applications using data from at least four of these disciplines: business, economics, social science, psychology, political science, administration of justice, life science, physical science, health science, information technology, and education
Technology-based statistical analysis










NoteCourse Objectives





Upon successful completion of the course, students will be able to:

Interpret data displayed in tables and graphs.
Apply concepts of sample space and probability.
Calculate measures of central tendency and variation for a data set.
Identify standard methods of obtaining data and the advantages and disadvantages of each.
Calculate the mean and variance of a discrete distribution.
Calculate probabilities using normal and t-distributions.
Distinguish between sample and population distributions and explain the role of the Central Limit Theorem.
Construct and interpret confidence intervals.
Determine and interpret statistical significance, including p-values.
Interpret output from a technology-based statistical analysis.
Explain hypothesis testing, including Type I and Type II errors.
Formulate hypothesis tests involving samples from one and two populations.
Select an appropriate technique for testing a hypothesis and interpret the result.
Use regression lines and ANOVA for estimation and inference, and interpret associated statistics.
Use appropriate statistical techniques to analyze and interpret applications based on data from at least four of the disciplines listed above.

title: Introduction Statistics
text:
2 Connections to Data Science:
This lesson connects introductory statistics with data science through prediction. Students use a regression model to estimate penguin body mass from flipper length, then investigate how visualization, data cleaning, sampling, and model choices affect the prediction.
Students consider how a model is built and interpreted, what makes a prediction useful, and why a model should not be treated as a perfect description of every individual.

title: Introduction Statistics
text:
3 Goals
By the end of this lesson, students will be able to:

Identify the explanatory variable (feature) and response variable (target).
Use a scatterplot and linear regression model to make a prediction.
Calculate and interpret a residual.
Explain why a predicted value will not accurately describe every individual with the same explanatory-variable value.
Describe how sample size, sampling bias, missing data, and outliers can affect predictions.
Distinguish interpolation from extrapolation.
Explain why association does not, by itself, demonstrate causation.
Consider whether one model is appropriate for different groups, such as different penguin species.

Driving question: How can we use regression to make a prediction, and how can we evaluate its reliability?

title: Introduction Statistics
text:
4 Activities

4.1 Introduction
Ask students to brainstorm five predictions people make in everyday life. Examples could include the weather, a sports result, college admission, or health risk. Record a few on the board.
Discuss:

What are we predicting?
What information might help us make the prediction?
What could make it inaccurate?
How is predicting different from describing data we have already collected?

Introduce the idea that a prediction is an estimate based on a model, not a guarantee about an individual.


4.2 Part 1: Build a Plot
















Ask students to identify:

The explanatory variable, or feature
The response variable, or target
The direction and form of the association
Any clusters, gaps, or unusual observations

Have students sketch or describe where they expect a regression line to fall before using technology to fit one.


4.3 Part 2: Fit and Interpret a Regression Model








After fitting our regression model, we found the equation of the best fit line to be \(y_{bm} = 49.68557x - 5780.83136\)
Ask students to record the model and explain:

What does the slope mean in the context of the problem?
What does the intercept represent in the context of the problem?
Does the intercept make logical sense for our penguins?
What does the model summarize, and what variation does it leave unexplained?



4.4 Part 3: Investigating The model
One penguin named Bertha has a flipper length of 195mm. Calculate the predicted value of her body mass (g) and then find the residual using the following equation.
residual = observed body mass − predicted body mass
Groups discuss:

Is the prediction higher or lower than the observed value?
Does every penguin with that flipper length have the predicted body mass? Why not?
Is the prediction interpolation or extrapolation?
What might change if the model is fit separately for each species?
Can the model be generalized to penguins beyond those represented in the data?



4.5 Part 4: Sampling and data reliability
Have students consider how the analysis might change if:

The sample included only a small number of penguins.
The sample came from one island or one species.
Rows with missing values were removed.
An unusual observation was excluded.
The model was used to predict outside the range of observed flipper lengths.

title: Differential Calculus
Differential Calculus
Differential Calculus
section: Connections to Data Science: Loss Functions and Optimization
text:
Connections to Data Science: Loss Functions and Optimization
Differential calculus helps us understand how a model can improve its predictions. A loss function measures the difference between a predicted value and the true value. We can measure this difference using absolute distance or squared distance; in linear regression, we commonly use the mean squared error, which averages the squared differences. The shape of the loss function matters: absolute-value loss has a sharp, pointy place where the derivative is not defined, while squared-error loss is smooth and easier to work with using calculus. Optimization is the process of finding the input values that make a function as small as possible. We begin with simple one-variable examples, where derivatives help us find minimum points, and then apply the same ideas to more complicated expressions involving vectors and matrices. Depending on its shape, a function may have one clear minimum, as in a convex landscape, or several possible low points, as in a nonconvex landscape. These ideas allow us to use calculus to minimize the mean squared error and find the line that best fits a set of data.

title: Integral Calculus
Integral Calculus
Integral Calculus
section: Connections to Data Science: Probability Theory and Convergence
text:
Connections to Data Science: Probability Theory and Convergence
Integral calculus helps us understand how quantities accumulate, which makes it useful for both probability and optimization. In gradient descent, ideas such as convexity and convergence can be introduced in a simple way: convex functions have a bowl-like shape, and when the steps are chosen appropriately, repeatedly moving downhill can bring us closer to a minimum. Integrals also allow us to find the total area under probability distributions, which must equal 1 because it represents the total probability. For example, exponential, Gamma, and Beta distributions can be integrated analytically to study probabilities and expected values. The normal distribution is different: its total area and probabilities cannot be expressed using an elementary antiderivative, so we approximate them numerically. This provides a natural connection between integration techniques and the numerical methods used in statistics, data science, and machine learning.

Introduction to Linear Algebra
section: Connections to Data Science: Correlation, Clustering, and PCA
text:
Connections to Data Science: Correlation, Clustering, and PCA
Linear algebra helps us represent and understand data using vectors, matrices, and geometric relationships. Correlation measures how two variables change together, and concepts such as dot products, centering, and normalization help us interpret that relationship. Clustering uses distances between data points to group observations that are similar, so students can connect geometric ideas about length and distance to the process of finding meaningful groups in a dataset. Singular value decomposition (SVD) then provides a way to break a matrix into simpler components that describe its most important patterns. Principal component analysis (PCA) uses these ideas to find new directions—called principal components—that capture the greatest variation in the data. Together, correlation, clustering, and SVD/PCA show how the basic tools of linear algebra can be used to measure similarity, discover structure, reduce complexity, and visualize high-dimensional data.

title: PreCalculus
PreCalculus
text:
2 Connections to Data Science: Functions
Precalculus provides a foundation for data science, machine learning, and AI by helping students understand how functions describe relationships in data. Students evaluate functions, work with graphs, compare linear and nonlinear relationships, and study exponential and logarithmic functions—tools that support modeling and prediction. Connecting these topics to explanatory and response variables, scatterplots, and data modeling gives students practice interpreting graphs and using models to make and assess predictions. These connections show how Precalculus prepares students to study data science and the mathematical ideas behind machine learning and AI.

title: PreCalculus
text:
3 Goals

Explain how functions can be introduced as models of data.
Connect the idea of input/output to explanatory/response variables.
Use real data sets to compare different function models.
Discuss limitations of using mathematical models for predictions.

title: PreCalculus
text:
4 Activity

4.1 Introduction
In Precalculus, we describe a function as a rule that assigns each input exactly one output. In data science, we can view functions as a model. A model is a simplified representation of data that describes patterns and allows us to make predictions.
In this lesson we will be using the Fish Market data set. This data set includes seven fish species and measurements such as their weight, length, height, and width. In this activity, students can use the physical features of the fish as input variables to predict a fish’s weight. This could be useful for fishermen, where measuring a fish’s length or width may be easier than weighing it. Students can compare linear and polynomial models to see which better represents the relationship between a fish’s measurements and its weight.
We also introduce the idea that real data does not always have perfect linear patterns, such as a fish that may gain weight faster than the length increases. We can then discuss how nonlinear models may be helpful in describing different types of patterns in data.


4.2 Part 1: Which function fits the fish?
Students compare linear, quadratic, power, and exponential models for predicting fish weight from length. Instructors discuss how visual fit, residual plots, and context guide model choice.
Can we estimate the weight of a fish based on its other physical features?









viewof input_species = Inputs.select(["Perch", "Bream", "Roach", "Pike", "Smelt", "Parkki", "Whitefish"])














We can begin with only two variables where x = length, and y = weight. We can show students a scatterplot of fish length vs. weight for different species of fish. We can then have a discussion about the plot.

What do you notice about the relationship between length and weight?
Is the relationship linear? Is it a function?
“Does the relationship change depending on species? What do you notice is different?”



4.3 Part 2: Now we can fit a linear model to our scatterplots and discuss what we notice.

viewof input_species2 = Inputs.select(["Perch", "Bream", "Roach", "Pike", "Smelt", "Parkki", "Whitefish"])














We can then have students examine a linear model and discuss. 1. For what species does the linear model accurately represent? 2. What does the slope mean in the context of the problem? 3. What does the y-intercept mean in the context of the problem? 4. Does the y-intercept make logical sense? 5. Does the line fit the model appropriately?


4.4 Part 3: Next, we will examine polynomial trend lines.

viewof input_species3 = Inputs.select(["Perch", "Bream", "Roach", "Pike", "Smelt", "Parkki", "Whitefish"])














Next, we can show students a polynomial trend line and discuss.

How does this trend line compare to the linear trend line?
Can we predict the length of a fish by using its weight?



4.5 Part 4: Transformed Variables
Students can also explore whether transforming a variable can make the relationship appear more linear. We can create new columns for (Length^2) and (Length^3), and plot the weight against each transformed variable. Students can compare the transformed graphs with the original plot and discuss which model looks more linear.

viewof input_species4 = Inputs.select(["Perch", "Bream", "Roach", "Pike", "Smelt", "Parkki", "Whitefish"])































Does plotting weight against (Length^2) or (Length^3) change the pattern?
Which graph appears to be the most linear?
Does a more linear graph make the predictions easier or more accurate?
Take note of which species of fish work well with the two different transformations.

title: PreCalculus
text:
5 Ethics and Equity Prompt
Students identify the observed range of lengths and predict weights inside and outside that range. They label predictions as interpolation or extrapolation and explain why extrapolation can be misleading.

title: PreCalculus
text:
6 Conclusion
After this lesson, students should now understand that functions can model relationships in the real world, and help us make predictions. Linear and quadratic models are simple examples of the types of models that can be used with machine learning. However, not all models are good models and are only approximations, so they may not always be accurate or make sense outside of the context of our data.
